```

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE, dpi = 100, fig.asp = 0.62, fig.width = 7,

library(mvgam)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(mvgam_theme(base_size = 12))

Eight economies, each observed for forty-nine years on the same three
outcomes, could share one vector autoregression (VAR) or have one each.
A single VAR for all eight ignores the differences between economies.
Eight separate VARs ignore what the economies have in common.
Forty-nine annual observations per economy also estimate a VAR poorly
on their own. A hierarchical VAR
gives each economy its own transition matrix and its own covariance of
shocks. It draws both towards a mean shared by all eight. The data
decide how strongly (Gelman and Hill
[2007](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511790942)).

Savage ([2016](https://rpubs.com/jimsavage/hierarchical_var)) fitted
such a model in Stan to growth in output, consumption and investment
for eight economies. This article fits it in mvgam to the same eight
economies over 1970 to 2019. It compares the pooling with Savage's
estimates, then works through what each economy's VAR offers: its
transition matrix, the correlation of its shocks, impulse responses,
variance decompositions and stability metrics.

## The data

The World Development Indicators (World Bank
[2024](https://data.worldbank.org/)) record annual GDP, final
consumption and gross fixed capital formation in constant local
currency. The WDI package (Arel-Bundock
[2013](https://doi.org/10.32614/RJ-2013-023)) downloads them for the
economies Savage used: Australia, Canada, Chile, Ireland, New Zealand,
South Africa, the United Kingdom and the United States.

```{r cache-path, include = FALSE}
# The download runs on the first knit. Later knits read the copy
# saved in the user's cache directory.
cache_file <- file.path(tools::R_user_dir("mvgam", "cache"),
                        "wdi_growth_1970_2019.rds")
```

```{r wdi, eval = !file.exists(cache_file)}
raw <- WDI::WDI(
  country = c("AU", "CA", "CL", "IE", "NZ", "ZA", "GB", "US"),
  indicator = c(gdp = "NY.GDP.MKTP.KN", cons = "NE.CON.TOTL.KN",
                gfcf = "NE.GDI.FTOT.KN"),
  start = 1970, end = 2019
)
```

```{r wdi-cache, include = FALSE}
if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  raw <- readRDS(cache_file)
} else {
  dir.create(dirname(cache_file), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  saveRDS(raw, cache_file)
}
```

The panel ends in 2019. The contractions and rebounds of the pandemic
years would dominate every estimate. Growth
is the difference in log levels from one year to the next, which
leaves 49 years for each economy:

```{r growth}
raw <- raw[order(raw$country, raw$year), ]
outcomes <- c(gdp = "GDP", cons = "Consumption", gfcf = "Investment")
growth <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(raw, raw$country), function(d) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(outcomes), function(v) {
    data.frame(country = d$country[-1], year = d$year[-1],
               outcome = outcomes[[v]], growth = diff(log(d[[v]])))
  }))
}))
growth$country <- factor(growth$country)
growth$outcome <- factor(growth$outcome, levels = outcomes)
growth$time <- growth$year - min(growth$year) + 1
rownames(growth) <- NULL
```

```{r plot-growth, fig.asp = 0.9, fig.cap = "Annual growth in real GDP, consumption and investment for the eight economies, 1971 to 2019, as the difference in log levels."}
ggplot(growth, aes(year, growth, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = palette.colors(8, "Okabe-Ito")) +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Growth (log difference)", colour = NULL)
```

```{r growth-numbers, include = FALSE}
sds <- tapply(growth$growth, growth$outcome, stats::sd)
fe_inv_ratio <- sprintf("%.0f", sds[["Investment"]] / sds[["GDP"]])
gdp09 <- growth[growth$outcome == "GDP" & growth$year == 2009, ]
fe_fell09 <- sum(gdp09$growth < 0)
# The largest rise in one outcome, as its country, year and percentage
top <- function(o) {
  r <- growth[growth$outcome == o, ]
  r <- r[which.max(r$growth), ]
  list(country = as.character(r$country), year = r$year,
       pct = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (exp(r$growth) - 1)))
}
top_gdp <- top("GDP")
top_inv <- top("Investment")
by_country <- tapply(growth$growth, growth$country, stats::sd)
volatile <- names(sort(by_country, decreasing = TRUE))[1:2]
```

Investment growth varies about `r fe_inv_ratio` times as much as GDP
growth. GDP fell in 2009 in `r fe_fell09` of the eight economies. The
largest rises in the panel are `r top_gdp$country`'s GDP growth of
`r top_gdp$pct` in `r top_gdp$year` and `r top_inv$country`'s
investment growth of `r top_inv$pct` in `r top_inv$year`.

Because the three outcomes differ in scale, one prior on the
coefficients would mean different things for each. Dividing each
outcome by its standard deviation over the whole panel puts them on one
scale, where a single prior means the same for all three. The
economies keep their own volatility. `r volatile[1]` and
`r volatile[2]` remain the most variable of the eight.

```{r standardise}
growth$y <- growth$growth / ave(growth$growth, growth$outcome, FUN = sd)
growth$y <- growth$y - ave(growth$y, growth$country, growth$outcome)
head(growth)
```

The second line subtracts each series' mean. Because an intercept for
each series and that series' latent states describe the same level,
estimating both leaves the pair poorly identified. The subtracted means
take the place of the intercepts Savage estimated for each economy and
outcome.

## The model

The model has two layers. The observation layer says that each
standardised growth rate $y_{c,o,t}$, for economy $c$, outcome $o$ and
year $t$, measures a latent state $z_{c,o,t}$ with observation error:

$$
y_{c,o,t} \sim \mathrm{Normal}(z_{c,o,t},\ \sigma).
$$

The three states of each economy follow a VAR of their own:

$$
\mathbf{z}_{c,t} \sim \mathrm{MVN}(A_c\,\mathbf{z}_{c,t-1},\ \Sigma_c),
\qquad
\Sigma_c = \mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\tau}_c)\,\Omega_c\,
  \mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\tau}_c).
$$

$A_c$ holds the lagged effects among economy $c$'s outcomes.
$\boldsymbol{\tau}_c$ holds the standard deviations of its shocks and
$\Omega_c$ their correlations. The economies do not interact: a shock
in Chile moves only Chile's states.

The pooling acts on both $A_c$ and $\Omega_c$. mvgam keeps every $A_c$
stationary through the prior of Heaps
([2023](https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.2022.2079648)), under which
each $A_c$ is a transformation of an unconstrained matrix. The
diagonal elements of the eight unconstrained matrices share one normal
prior. Their off-diagonal elements share another. mvgam estimates the
means and precisions of both priors. The correlation of each
economy's shocks mixes a correlation shared by all eight with a
deviation of its own:

$$
\Omega_c = \alpha\,\Omega + (1 - \alpha)\,\tilde\Omega_c .
$$

With $\alpha$ near one, every economy's shocks correlate as $\Omega$
says. With $\alpha$ near zero, each economy's correlation is its own.
Ben Goodrich proposed this mixture in the discussion of Savage's post.
We kept the priors given there. The global correlation keeps mvgam's
default LKJ(1) prior, which is uniform over correlation matrices. Each
deviation $\tilde\Omega_c$ has an LKJ(10) prior, which holds it near
the identity (Lewandowski et al.
[2009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmva.2009.04.008)). $\alpha$ has a
Beta(2, 2) prior.

Savage fitted the VAR to the observed growth rates. Because
statistical agencies revise national accounts after their first
release, a published growth rate measures the economy with error of
its own. The state-space layer keeps that measurement error apart from
the economies' shocks (Auger-Méthé et al.
[2021](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecm.1470)). Forty-nine years of data
separate the two variances poorly. The inverse gamma prior on $\sigma$
supplies the missing information, placing observation error near 0.16
of a standard deviation of growth.

In mvgam, `VAR()` takes the grouping through two arguments. `gr`
names the factor whose levels each get a VAR, here the economies.
`subgr` names the factor whose levels are the states within each
group, here the outcomes. `cor = TRUE` estimates the correlations of
the shocks:

```{r fit}
fit <- mvgam(
  formula = y ~ -1,
  trend_formula = ~ VAR(p = 1, gr = country, subgr = outcome, cor = TRUE),
  family = gaussian(),
  data = growth,
  priors = c(
    prior(inv_gamma(20, 3), class = sigma),
    prior(lkj_corr_cholesky(10), class = L_deviation_group_trend),
    prior(beta(2, 2), class = alpha_cor_trend)
  ),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  seed = 2016,
  silent = 2
)
```

The observation formula `y ~ -1` adds nothing to the latent states.
mvgam names each of the 24 series by joining its economy and outcome,
as in `Australia_GDP`.

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
# Format an estimate with its interval for inline reporting
ci <- function(est, lo, hi, digits = 2) {
  # A value that rounds to zero prints without a minus sign
  f <- function(v) sub("^-(0\\.0+)$", "\\1",
                       formatC(v, format = "f", digits = digits))
  paste0(f(est), " [", f(lo), ", ", f(hi), "]")
}
```

## How strongly the economies pool

`alpha_cor_trend` is the weight $\alpha$ on the shared correlation:

```{r alpha, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "Posterior distribution of the weight on the shared correlation of the shocks."}
mcmc_plot(fit, variable = "alpha_cor_trend", type = "hist")
```

```{r alpha-numbers, include = FALSE}
alpha <- as.numeric(as_draws_matrix(fit, variable = "alpha_cor_trend"))
fe_alpha <- ci(mean(alpha), quantile(alpha, 0.025), quantile(alpha, 0.975))
```

The weight is `r fe_alpha`. Savage estimated 0.82 [0.75, 0.90] from
313 annual observations of an earlier vintage of the same indicators.

`residual_cor()` summarises the shared correlation $\Omega$.
`covariance = "innovation"` asks for the correlation of the shocks
themselves. The default, `"stationary"`, passes them through each
economy's transition matrix:

```{r rc-global}
rc <- residual_cor(fit, covariance = "innovation")
summary(rc)
```

```{r rc-numbers, include = FALSE}
pair <- function(rc, a, b) {
  s <- summary(rc)
  r <- s[(s$series_1 == a & s$series_2 == b) |
           (s$series_1 == b & s$series_2 == a), ]
  ci(r$Estimate, r$Q_lower, r$Q_upper)
}
fe_gc <- pair(rc, "GDP", "Consumption")
fe_gi <- pair(rc, "GDP", "Investment")
fe_ci <- pair(rc, "Consumption", "Investment")
est <- rc$cor
```

GDP shocks correlate with investment shocks at `r fe_gi` and with
consumption shocks at `r fe_gc`. Consumption and investment shocks
correlate at `r fe_ci`. Savage's estimates were 0.93, 0.89 and 0.74,
in the same order.

`by_group = TRUE` returns the correlation of each economy's shocks:

```{r rc-groups, fig.width = 8, fig.asp = 0.8, fig.cap = "Posterior mean correlations of the shocks in each economy. Outlined pairs have 95% credible intervals that exclude zero."}
rc_groups <- residual_cor(fit, covariance = "innovation", by_group = TRUE)
plot(rc_groups, include_global = FALSE)
```

```{r rc-group-numbers, include = FALSE}
gi <- vapply(names(rc_groups)[-1], function(g) {
  rc_groups[[g]]$cor["GDP", "Investment"]
}, numeric(1))
fe_gi_range <- sprintf("%.2f", range(gi))
n_below <- sum(gi < est["GDP", "Investment"])
fe_below <- if (n_below == length(gi)) {
  "Every economy's correlation is below the shared one."
} else {
  paste0(n_below, " of the eight economies' correlations are below the ",
         "shared one.")
}
```

The economies' GDP and investment shocks correlate at
`r fe_gi_range[1]` to `r fe_gi_range[2]`, against the shared
`r sprintf("%.2f", est["GDP", "Investment"])`. `r fe_below` Forty-nine
years of
shocks move each deviation little from the identity its LKJ(10) prior
favours. The fifth of each economy's correlation that the deviation
contributes pulls that correlation towards zero.

## Transition matrices

`posterior_transition_matrix()` with `groups = "all"` returns each
economy's $A_c$. Its diagonal holds the persistence of each outcome
from one year to the next:

```{r A-diag, fig.asp = 0.8, fig.cap = "Posterior means and 95% credible intervals of the diagonal of each economy's transition matrix."}
A_all <- posterior_transition_matrix(fit, groups = "all")
plot(A_all, type = "diagonal")
```

```{r A-numbers, include = FALSE}
A <- posterior_transition_matrix(fit)
cell <- function(m, i, j) ci(m$A[i, j], m$A_lower[i, j], m$A_upper[i, j])
fe_cons_pool <- cell(A, "Consumption", "Consumption")
fe_gdp_pool <- cell(A, "GDP", "GDP")
us <- A_all[["United States"]]
fe_us_gdp <- cell(us, "GDP", "GDP")
fe_us_cons <- cell(us, "GDP", "Consumption")
# The stationary correlation of the states, the regressors of each VAR
states <- residual_cor(fit, by_group = TRUE)
gdp_cons <- vapply(names(states)[-1], function(g) {
  states[[g]]$cor["GDP", "Consumption"]
}, numeric(1))
fe_us_states <- sprintf("%.2f", gdp_cons[["United States"]])
most_persistent <- tolower(rownames(A$A)[which.max(diag(A$A))])
us_rank <- rank(-gdp_cons)[["United States"]]
fe_us_rank <- if (us_rank == 1) {
  "the most strongly of the eight"
} else {
  paste0("ranked ", us_rank, " of the eight")
}
```

Without `groups`, `posterior_transition_matrix()` averages the eight
matrices in each posterior draw:

```{r A}
A
```

On average, `r most_persistent` growth is the most persistent of the
three outcomes. The average diagonal coefficient is `r fe_cons_pool`
for consumption and `r fe_gdp_pool` for GDP.

Consider the United States. Its GDP diagonal is `r fe_us_gdp` and
its GDP growth loads on last year's consumption growth at
`r fe_us_cons`. In the United States, the states of GDP and
consumption correlate at `r fe_us_states`, `r fe_us_rank`. Last
year's GDP and consumption then carry nearly the same information
about this year. The model can trade a negative coefficient on one
against a positive coefficient on the other. The wide intervals record
that trade-off.

## Impulse responses

An impulse response gives the expected path of every state after a
single shock to one of them (Lütkepohl
[2005](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-27752-1)). `irf()` computes
the generalised impulse response by default (Pesaran and Shin
[1998](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(97)00214-0)). A shock to one
outcome brings with it the shocks its correlated outcomes receive in
the same year. Horizon 1 is the year of the shock.

```{r irf}
irfs <- irf(fit, h = 8)
```

`plot()` selects the shock and the responses among the 24 states by
name. Here we draw the responses of the three Australian states to a
shock in Australian investment:

```{r plot-irf, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "Generalised impulse responses of Australian GDP, consumption and investment to a one standard deviation shock in Australian investment, with 95% credible intervals."}
aus <- c("Australia_GDP", "Australia_Consumption", "Australia_Investment")
plot(irfs, series = "Australia_Investment", responses = aus)
```

```{r irf-numbers, include = FALSE}
ir <- as.data.frame(irfs)
resp <- function(shock, h) {
  r <- ir[ir$shock == shock & ir$horizon == h, ]
  ci(r$irfQ50, r$irfQ2.5, r$irfQ97.5)
}
fe_ir_ii1 <- resp("Australia_Investment -> Australia_Investment", 1)
fe_ir_ig1 <- resp("Australia_Investment -> Australia_GDP", 1)
fe_ir_ic2 <- resp("Australia_Investment -> Australia_Consumption", 2)
from_inv <- ir[startsWith(ir$shock, "Australia_Investment ->"), ]
settled <- vapply(seq_len(8), function(h) {
  all(abs(from_inv$irfQ50[from_inv$horizon >= h]) < 0.01)
}, logical(1))
fe_settle <- if (any(settled)) {
  paste0("Every response stays within 0.01 of zero from year ",
         which(settled)[1], ".")
} else {
  "Some responses stay above 0.01 at year eight."
}
```

The shock raises Australian investment by `r fe_ir_ii1` standard
deviations in its first year. Because investment and GDP shocks
correlate, GDP moves with it, by `r fe_ir_ig1`. In the second year
consumption is at `r fe_ir_ic2`. `r fe_settle`

## Variance decompositions

A forecast error variance decomposition (FEVD) splits the variance of
each state's forecast among the states whose shocks generate it, at
each horizon. `fevd()` splits the variance with the Cholesky factor of
each economy's $\Sigma_c$, taken in the order of the levels of
`outcome`. Where two outcomes' shocks correlate, the factor assigns
the shared part to the outcome that comes first, here GDP.

```{r fevd, fig.width = 8, fig.asp = 0.45, fig.cap = "Median share of the forecast error variance of each Australian outcome that each Australian source of shocks generates, by forecast horizon."}
fevds <- fevd(fit, h = 8)
plot(fevds, series = aus, contributing = aus)
```

```{r fevd-numbers, include = FALSE}
fv <- as.data.frame(fevds)
share <- function(shock, h) {
  r <- fv[fv$shock == shock & fv$horizon == h, ]
  sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r$fevdQ50)
}
fe_fv_gi1 <- share("Australia_GDP -> Australia_Investment", 1)
fe_fv_gc8 <- share("Australia_GDP -> Australia_Consumption", 8)
fe_fv_gg8 <- share("Australia_GDP -> Australia_GDP", 8)
```

In the first year, GDP shocks generate `r fe_fv_gi1` of the forecast
variance of Australian investment. That share is the part of two
correlated shocks the ordering assigns to GDP. The shares barely move
with the horizon. At eight years GDP shocks generate `r fe_fv_gg8` of
the forecast variance of GDP itself and `r fe_fv_gc8` of that of
consumption. Reordering the levels of `outcome` and refitting would
move the shared part of each correlated pair to the other outcome. The
generalised impulse responses above are the same in any order.

## Stability of each economy

`stability()` summarises each economy's $A_c$ as the stability metrics
of Ives et al.
([2003](https://doi.org/10.1890/0012-9615(2003)073[0301:ECSAEI]2.0.CO;2)).
Reactivity is the log of the largest singular value of $A_c$. Above
zero, some perturbation grows in the year after it occurs before the
economy returns towards its means (Neubert et al.
[2009](https://doi.org/10.1890/08-2014.1)). The mean return rate is
the largest modulus of the eigenvalues of $A_c$. Once the slowest mode
dominates, a deviation shrinks by about this factor each year. The
variance return rate is its square. On a hierarchical fit,
`stability()` reports these three metrics for every economy:

```{r stability, fig.width = 8, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "Posterior medians and 95% credible intervals of reactivity and of the mean and variance return rates of each economy. The dashed line marks zero reactivity."}
stab <- stability(fit)
plot(stab)
```

```{r stability-numbers, include = FALSE}
st <- function(g, m) {
  r <- stab[stab$group == g & stab$metric == m, ]
  ci(r$Estimate, r$Q2.5, r$Q97.5)
}
react <- stab[stab$metric == "reactivity", ]
fe_us_react <- st("United States", "reactivity")
mrr <- stab[stab$metric == "mean_return_rate", ]
fe_mrr_range <- sprintf("%.2f", range(mrr$Estimate))
n_halve <- sum(mrr$Estimate^2 < 0.5)
fe_halve <- if (n_halve == nrow(mrr)) {
  "in every economy"
} else {
  paste0("in ", n_halve, " of the eight economies")
}
above <- as.character(react$group[react$Q2.5 > 0])
fe_react <- if (length(above) == 0) {
  "No economy has a reactivity interval above zero."
} else {
  paste0("Reactivity intervals lie above zero for ",
         knitr::combine_words(above), ".")
}
```

The median mean return rates run from `r fe_mrr_range[1]` to
`r fe_mrr_range[2]`. A deviation of growth from its mean halves within
two years `r fe_halve`. `r fe_react` The United States has a
reactivity of `r fe_us_react`, shaped by the large offsetting
coefficients of its transition matrix.

Partial pooling puts four fifths of the weight on a correlation of
shocks shared by all eight economies, close to Savage's estimate from
an earlier vintage of the same data. Each economy keeps a transition
matrix of its own. Its coefficients are least certain where two
states move together, as the GDP and consumption states of the United
States do.
Forty-nine annual observations are few for a VAR of three states. The
shared means make eight of them estimable at once.
